new_statements.rule_in_words: Chatelain's transcription convention: the 'tonic accent' is on the penultimate syllable by default and is left unmarked there; any word whose accent is not on the penult carries an acute accent on the accented vowel (his example nsófulu 'lung', accent on the antepenult, is the U-Iaa word on p. 64). In the U-Iaka column many words are marked with a final accent (n-zíu 'eye', kuó 'hand', n-gáa 'medicine-man', n-sá 'antelope', n-zó 'house', m-vuá 'dog', n-gó 'leopard', n-kué 'lion', (li)-buó 'knee', ku-láuza 'to cook', mu-bíi 'hunter'), so the 'exceptions' are numerous; in a Teke B70 language these marks almost certainly record high tone rather than stress. The statement is an orthographic note for a 19th-century comparative wordlist, not a phonological analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-penult accent is treated as a lexical exception marked with an acute accent (example nsófulu); the U-Iaka vocabulary itself shows many final-accented items (see rule_in_words).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in a comparative vocabulary (English-Portuguese-Kimbundu-U-Iaka, pp. 63-67). The convention is stated once for the whole set of 'Notes and Vocabularies' (originally devised for Kimbundu) and is applied to the U-Iaka column. The grammatical notes (pp. 60-61: noun classes, concords, pronouns, possessives, copula, t > r) say nothing about accent or tone; the words 'tone' and 'stress' do not occur in the paper. The modern description of the language (Mouandza 2002 PhD abstract) treats its phonology 'en priorité' as a tonology, so the 'tonic accent' here should be read as an impressionistic pitch/prominence mark on a tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened source is Chatelain 1894 on 'U-Iaka' / 'Ma-Iaka', whose informant was said to be a Yaka of the lower Kwango (which would be Yaka H31 [yaf], yaka1269, DRC/Angola); Maho's EBALL note carried by Glottolog (ref 61618) judges that 'the data match Ki-Teke B73c = Yaka (Congo) [iyx]' and Glottolog files the paper under yaka1274. The modern descriptions (Mouandza 1991, 2002) call the language 'iyaa' and note its classification is contested (Koongo for some authors, Teke for others). The 1894 vocabulary is a comparative Kimbundu/U-Iaka list collected at Loanda, not fieldwork in the Lekoumou.
